sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Core, database and AI package list
sections.what: Lists the packages for the web framework, the database, the background job system, the AI and language tools, the vector search, and the data and text tools.
sections.why: Each group provides a part of the platform's features.
sections.watch_out: Large packages here make the install slow and can fail on some computers.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Monitoring, utilities and testing package list
sections.what: Lists packages for logging and error reporting, small helpers such as environment reading, Word and Excel and PDF creation, and the testing tools.
sections.why: Supports the rest of the app, including exports and automated tests.
sections.watch_out: The testing tools are installed in production too, which adds size and risk.

summary: The list of Python packages the backend needs, each pinned to one exact version.
purpose: Makes sure everyone installs the same package versions so the app behaves the same.
why: Likely reason: the AI and data libraries change fast, so pinned versions prevent surprise breaks.
how: The installer reads each line and installs that exact version. The list is grouped by purpose: the web core, the database, the background jobs, the AI libraries, the language and data tools, text handling, web requests, security, logging, utilities and testing.
inputs: The pinned names and versions in this file.
outputs: An installed set of Python packages in the environment.
risks: Some packages are very large, such as torch, and some older pins may not install on new Python versions. The list repeats a few packages, such as python-multipart and httpx.
debug: If install fails, read the first error and find which package and version it names. Check that the Python version matches the one in the Dockerfile. Try installing the failing package alone to see its message.
